DiffuPlan: Editable Planning State for Diffusion Language Model Agents

Qisheng Zhou Affiliation: New York University Shanghai    Zhen Xiong Affiliation: New York University    Qiaoyu Tan ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: New York University Shanghai
Abstract

Diffusion language models (dLLMs) are emerging as an alternative to autoregressive (AR) language models, yet dLLM agents largely inherit an interaction protocol designed for AR generation: once intermediate state is written, later observations can only be incorporated by appending more text. This is a poor match to a defining capability of dLLMs—reconstructing earlier text conditioned on context that appears both before and after it. We ask whether this capability can support a different agent-state paradigm in which intermediate planning state is directly revisable as evidence arrives. We introduce DiffuPlan, a diffusion search agent that maintains a single editable planning state and reconstructs only the affected steps when later evidence resolves an entity or changes the search route. To support variable-length revisions, we introduce Expansion-Partition Marginalization (EPM), which marginalizes over equivalent expansion paths. We further adapt diffusion trajectory RL to multi-turn search. Across four multi-hop QA benchmarks, DiffuPlan achieves 50.24 average F1, outperforming strong AR search agents. More importantly, under identical data and training, editable planning state improves the diffusion agent by 2.44 F1 versus only 0.47 for its AR source model. These results show that dLLMs need not imitate append-only AR agents: revising committed state is a distinct agentic advantage.11 1 Code is available at https://github.com/Jaasssoooonnnnn/DiffuPlan.

1 Introduction

Language agents act over multiple turns, continually forming and revising intermediate hypotheses, subgoals, and plans as new observations arrive. Yet the textual state of most agents is effectively append-only: once a model writes an intermediate decision, later evidence does not change that text; instead, the agent expresses the revision by generating additional text. This interaction pattern is natural for autoregressive (AR) language models, which generate a continuation conditioned on a fixed prefix. It is not obviously natural for diffusion language models (dLLMs).

dLLMs provide a different computational primitive. Rather than committing every token strictly left-to-right, masked and block-diffusion language models can reconstruct selected positions from surrounding context (Nie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025; Arriola et al., 2025; Bie et al., 2025). This raises a basic question for agent design: should a diffusion agent inherit the same append-only state paradigm as an AR agent, or should its intermediate state itself remain editable?

Existing dLLM agents largely follow the former design. They retain ReAct-style, append-only interaction histories (Yao et al., 2023) and use diffusion primarily to accelerate or restructure forward generation—for example, by issuing tool calls from partially denoised states or overlapping reasoning with tool execution (Zhao et al., 2026; Jünger et al., 2026). Under such an interaction, the distinctive reconstruction capability of dLLMs is not used to revise agent state across turns. In our controlled setting, this mismatch is visible empirically: with the same training data and post-training recipe, a search agent built on LLaDA2.0-mini reaches 47.80 average F1 under append-only plan revision, below 49.54 for Ling-mini-2.0 (Ling Team, 2025), the AR model from which LLaDA2.0-mini was converted (Bie et al., 2025).

Multi-hop search provides a natural testbed for studying this mismatch. During search, later evidence routinely changes state formed earlier: a retrieved passage can resolve an entity referenced by a pending subquestion, add constraints that make a query more specific, or invalidate the planned search route. Making this state explicit and revisable helps even without training: on our validation set, prompting the untrained LLaDA2.0-mini yields 26.53 F1 without a plan, 28.61 with an initial plan, and 29.26 when the plan is revised as evidence arrives. Existing agents can represent such changes, but typically by appending another rationale or a regenerated plan (Luo et al., 2026). Consequently, multiple versions of the same intermediate state may coexist in the interaction history. In contrast, a diffusion agent could maintain a single current state and revise the affected content where it was originally written, using later evidence as conditioning context.

We introduce DiffuPlan, a diffusion search agent with an editable planning state. The plan is treated not merely as another piece of historical text, but as a persistent state variable that should reflect the agent’s current search strategy. When later evidence resolves an intermediate answer or changes the route, the agent requests an edit and reconstructs only the affected plan span conditioned on the preserved plan and the subsequent interaction. This turns cross-turn state revision into a native reconstruction problem for the dLLM.

Making this idea trainable raises two central technical challenges. First, one shared model must support two different computation patterns: forward action generation should remain block-causal, whereas state revision must condition on later evidence. We therefore use a block-causal Action Mode and a full-canvas Edit Mode with shared parameters. Second, revisions are often variable-length. Dynamic expansion allows an editable mask to grow, but the same target replacement may be realized by many equally valid expansion paths. We introduce Expansion-Partition Marginalization (EPM), which marginalizes over these paths and supervises the final edit rather than an arbitrary expansion trajectory. SFT teaches action generation and state reconstruction jointly, and we further optimize search decisions from end-task reward with Multi-turn Diffusion Search with Anchored Stabilization (MDSAS), which extends TraceRL (Wang et al., 2026) to multi-turn search and stabilizes training with a frozen SFT anchor.

The central empirical question is not merely whether editable plans improve QA, but whether they provide a diffusion-specific advantage. Our controlled 2×22\times 2 comparison varies both backbone (diffusion vs. its AR source model) and state protocol (editable vs. append-only) under matched data and training. Editable state improves the dLLM by 2.44 F1, compared with only 0.47 F1 for the AR model, while reducing generated tokens for both. Moreover, the diffusion gain is mechanism-aligned: it is only 0.20 F1 when no edit is requested, but rises to 4.63 F1 with multiple updates and 7.12 F1 when replanning is required.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We identify a mismatch between the append-only state paradigm inherited from AR agents and the cross-context reconstruction capability of dLLMs, and formulate editable planning state as a diffusion-native alternative for multi-turn agents.

  • •

    We introduce DiffuPlan, which realizes cross-turn state revision with shared Action/Edit modes and learns variable-length edits with EPM, marginalizing over equivalent expansion paths.

  • •

    We show through matched backbone–protocol comparisons that editable state benefits the diffusion agent substantially more than its AR counterpart, with gains increasing as more revision is required, while DiffuPlan also achieves the best average F1 among the evaluated search agents.

2 Related Work

Search agents and evolving intermediate state.

Retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2023) has developed into search agents that interleave reasoning with retrieval and decide what evidence to acquire next. IRCoT and ReAct alternate reasoning and search (Trivedi et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023); Search-R1 and R1-Searcher learn search behavior with reinforcement learning (Jin et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025); Search-o1 refines retrieved evidence during long-form reasoning (Li et al., 2025). A complementary line of work makes intermediate state more explicit. Plan∗RAG represents dependencies among retrieval steps (Verma et al., 2024), D2Plan revises subquestions and plans from retrieval feedback (Luo et al., 2026), and SLEUTH tracks facts, hypotheses, and open questions through successive structured states (Liu, 2026). These methods recognize that search state evolves, but their revisions are still serialized as newly generated text. DiffuPlan instead treats the current plan as a persistent state variable and directly reconstructs the affected earlier span after later evidence arrives.

Diffusion language models and text revision.

Masked and block-diffusion language models generate by iterative denoising rather than strictly token-by-token continuation (Nie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025; Arriola et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Bie et al., 2025). This makes reconstruction and editing natural operations. DreamOn introduces expansion and deletion states for variable-length infilling, while LLaDA2.1 revises previously committed tokens during block-diffusion generation (Wu et al., 2026; Bie et al., 2026). These works revise text within a single generation. Our setting is different: an agent first commits a state, interacts with an external environment, receives new evidence in later turns, and then revises the earlier state conditioned on that evidence. We study this cross-turn revision as an agent-state primitive.

Diffusion language models for agents and post-training.

Recent work begins to adapt dLLMs to tool use and search. DLLM-Searcher combines SFT and preference optimization with P-ReAct, using partially denoised states to trigger retrieval early (Zhao et al., 2026), while SARDI forms retrieval queries from tentative denoising states (Jünger et al., 2026). TraceRL optimizes denoising trajectories with reinforcement learning (Wang et al., 2026). These methods exploit diffusion during forward response generation, but the interaction history itself remains append-only. DiffuPlan is complementary: its central question is whether diffusion reconstruction can be used to revise agent state that was written in an earlier turn.

3 DiffuPlan

DiffuPlan treats planning as a mutable state-transition process. Let HtH_{t} denote the interaction history available at turn tt and let PtP_{t} denote the agent’s current planning state, represented by a single plan embedded at a fixed location in that history. Standard append-only agents leave earlier plan text unchanged and express a revision by generating another version later in the sequence. DiffuPlan instead maintains the invariant that PtP_{t} is the unique current plan: later evidence may trigger a state transition Pt→Pt+1P_{t}\rightarrow P_{t+1} that replaces only the affected span at its original position. The same dLLM implements both forward interaction and state reconstruction through two attention modes (Figure 2).

3.1 Editable Planning State

Planning state and actions.

The initial plan decomposes a question into indexed subquestions #Q_i. A future step may refer to an unresolved intermediate answer through #A_i. At each turn, Action Mode generates reasoning followed by one of four terminal actions: search retrieves evidence, update binds a resolved intermediate answer into the plan, replan revises upcoming steps, and answer terminates the interaction. The two edit operations, update and replan, change the planning state rather than append a second plan.

Formally, given question qq and history HtH_{t}, Action Mode generates the next segment ztz_{t} block by block under block-causal attention MactM^{\mathrm{act}}:

zt∼πactθ(⋅∣q,Ht;Mact),(at,ut)=terminal⁡(zt),\begin{gathered}z_{t}\sim\pi^{\mathrm{act}}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q,H_{t};M^{\mathrm{act}}),\\ (a_{t},u_{t})=\operatorname{terminal}(z_{t}),\end{gathered} (1)

where at∈{search,update,replan,answer}a_{t}\in\{\texttt{search},\texttt{update},\texttt{replan},\texttt{answer}\} and utu_{t} is its payload. A search appends a retrieved observation to the environment history. An update or replan instead hands control to Edit Mode before the next Action-Mode segment is generated.

Cross-turn state reconstruction.

The key asymmetry is temporal: the plan span to be revised appears before the evidence that motivates its revision. Controller Γ\Gamma maps an edit request (at,ut)(a_{t},u_{t}) to one or more editable spans in PtP_{t}. Edit Mode forms a full canvas XtX_{t} containing the original plan, subsequent actions and observations, and the triggering edit request, then masks only the selected plan content. Under full-canvas attention MeditM^{\mathrm{edit}}, the masked span can condition simultaneously on preserved plan context and on evidence that arrived later. The reconstructed text is committed at the original location, yielding the new state Pt+1P_{t+1} while leaving unselected state and the surrounding interaction unchanged.

For a replan that opens the suffix beginning at a selected step, write Pt=Ptkeep⊕PtopenP_{t}=P_{t}^{\mathrm{keep}}\oplus P_{t}^{\mathrm{open}}. Edit Mode reconstructs P^topen\widehat{P}_{t}^{\mathrm{open}} and commits

Pt+1=Ptkeep⊕P^topen.P_{t+1}=P_{t}^{\mathrm{keep}}\oplus\widehat{P}_{t}^{\mathrm{open}}. (2)

An update is a localized special case: the selected answer marker is reconstructed with its resolved value, which is then propagated to identical unresolved references in the plan. Appendix A gives the complete execution loop and Appendix B specifies localization and commit semantics.

Dynamic expansion.

State revisions need not preserve length. A placeholder may expand into a multi-token entity name, and replanning may replace a short subquestion with a more specific or longer continuation. We therefore allow an editable mask either to emit a token or to emit χexp=⟨EXPAND⟩\chi_{\mathrm{exp}}=\langle\mathrm{EXPAND}\rangle, which replaces that mask with two masks carrying the same owner label. Repeated fill-or-expand operations support length-preserving and length-growing edits without reserving a fixed-size canvas.

3.2 Learning Variable-Length State Revision

Joint SFT teaches two complementary behaviors from the same teacher trajectories. An action record supervises the next Action-Mode segment given the current interaction history. An edit record supervises the desired replacement given a masked earlier plan, the later evidence, and the triggering edit request. The two record types share parameters but use the attention pattern of their corresponding runtime mode.

Why expansion creates ambiguous supervision.

Dynamic expansion introduces a latent-path problem. Suppose two active masks must reconstruct four target tokens (y1,y2,y3,y4)(y_{1},y_{2},y_{3},y_{4}). The target edit is unique, but the four tokens can be allocated to the two masks as (1,3)(1,3), (2,2)(2,2), or (3,1)(3,1). These allocations imply different immediate labels—for example, (y1,χexp)(y_{1},\chi_{\mathrm{exp}}) versus (χexp,χexp)(\chi_{\mathrm{exp}},\chi_{\mathrm{exp}})—even though they can lead to exactly the same final replacement. Standard single-path cross-entropy chooses one allocation as the target and therefore penalizes other valid expansion decisions.

Expansion-Partition Marginalization.

EPM removes this arbitrary choice by marginalizing over all valid allocations. Let 𝒰e\mathcal{U}_{e} be the contiguous unresolved components of edit record ee. Component cc has target sequence y(c)y^{(c)} of length ncn_{c}, mcm_{c} active masks, and 𝒫c\mathcal{P}_{c}, the set of positive mcm_{c}-part compositions of ncn_{c}. For a composition 𝜿\boldsymbol{\kappa}, mask ii is supervised with the corresponding target token when κi=1\kappa_{i}=1 and with χexp\chi_{\mathrm{exp}} otherwise. Let X~e,c\widetilde{X}_{e,c} be the full canvas at the current editing step, in which some target tokens of component cc may already be resolved, and let ii index its active masks. The edit objective is

Joint SFT.

The Action-Mode objective ℓact\ell_{\mathrm{act}} is the standard denoising loss over corrupted positions in the newly generated segment. We optimize action and edit records jointly:

SFT therefore learns how to produce executable actions and how to realize a requested state revision.

3.3 Optimizing Multi-Turn Search Decisions

SFT imitates teacher actions along teacher trajectories, but the agent must also learn when to search, update, replan, or answer under its own rollouts. We therefore further optimize these decisions with MDSAS, which adapts TraceRL (Wang et al., 2026) from single-response diffusion generation to multi-turn search. Importantly, this stage optimizes Action-Mode decisions; Edit-Mode reconstruction remains supervised by SFT.

For each question with answer aliases 𝒴⋆\mathcal{Y}^{\star}, we sample GG complete trajectories {τg}g=1G\{\tau_{g}\}_{g=1}^{G}. The terminal reward is answer F1 multiplied by a format-validity gate and is normalized within each question group to obtain a trajectory-level advantage. As in TraceRL, rollout records the denoising step at which each Action-Mode token is committed. We group every few commit steps of a block into a slice xg,kx_{g,k}, and evaluate the tokens committed in each slice given the tokens committed before it. The resulting clipped policy-gradient objective is denoted ℒRLact\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RL}}^{\mathrm{act}}; full details are given in Appendix C.4.

Frozen-reference stabilization.

Multi-turn agent RL introduces a failure mode not addressed by a moving old-policy reference: once all rollouts in a group become structurally invalid, their rewards have no variance and the policy receives no signal that restores the executable action format. As in KL-regularized RL fine-tuning (Ouyang et al., 2022; Shao et al., 2024), we therefore regularize every rollout slice toward the frozen SFT policy θSFT\theta_{\mathrm{SFT}}. Let

ug,k,j=log⁡pθSFT,g,k,j−log⁡pθ,g,k,j,u_{g,k,j}=\log p_{\theta_{\mathrm{SFT}},g,k,j}-\log p_{\theta,g,k,j}, (5)

and h⁡(u)=exp⁡(u)−1−uh(u)=\exp(u)-1-u. The final objective is

ℒanchor\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{anchor}} =𝔼Ωall​[h⁡(ug,k,j)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\Omega_{\mathrm{all}}}[h(u_{g,k,j})], (6)
ℒMDSAS\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MDSAS}} =ℒRLact+λSFT​ℒanchor.\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RL}}^{\mathrm{act}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{SFT}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{anchor}}.

The anchor is a training stabilization mechanism rather than the core state-revision contribution; Section 5.4 quantifies its effect.

4 Experiments

Our experiments answer four questions: RQ1: Does DiffuPlan provide competitive end-to-end multi-hop search performance? RQ2: Does editable planning state benefit a diffusion backbone more than an otherwise matched AR backbone? RQ3: Does the benefit increase on examples that require more state revision, as predicted by our hypothesis? RQ4: Are EPM, dynamic expansion, and the frozen SFT anchor necessary for learning and optimizing the editable-state agent?

4.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks.

We evaluate on four open-domain multi-hop QA benchmarks in which later evidence can change earlier intermediate state: 500 sampled questions each from HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018), 2WikiMultiHopQA (2Wiki) (Ho et al., 2020), and MuSiQue (Trivedi et al., 2022), plus all 125 Bamboogle (Press et al., 2023) questions. Teacher trajectories are collected only from the HotpotQA and 2Wiki training splits; MuSiQue and Bamboogle therefore test transfer beyond the teacher-trajectory domains.

Baselines and controlled protocol.

Inference-only baselines include Direct, CoT (Kojima et al., 2022), Standard RAG (Lewis et al., 2020), SuRe (Kim et al., 2024), Selective-Context (Li et al., 2023), Iter-RetGen (Shao et al., 2023), and IRCoT (Trivedi et al., 2023), all using the unmodified LLaDA2.0-mini checkpoint. We compare against AR search agents Search-o1 (Li et al., 2025), Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025), and R1-Searcher (Song et al., 2025), using their released systems. For DLLM-Searcher (Zhao et al., 2026), we migrate its complete post-training pipeline, including SFT and Variance-Reduced Preference Optimization (VRPO), to LLaDA2.0-mini and use its P-ReAct inference procedure. All retrieval-capable systems query the same frozen E5/Wiki18 index.

To test the central hypothesis independently of overall system differences, we additionally construct a matched 2×22\times 2 comparison: {editable, append-only} planning state on {LLaDA2.0-mini, Ling-mini-2.0}. Ling-mini-2.0 (Ling Team, 2025) is the AR model from which LLaDA2.0-mini was converted (Bie et al., 2025), with the same architecture, parameter count, and tokenizer; the four agents use the same teacher trajectories, SFT schedule, MDSAS recipe, retriever, retrieval budget, and checkpoint-selection protocol. This comparison isolates whether the state protocol interacts specifically with the diffusion backbone.

Metrics.

Token F1 is our primary answer metric, following R1-Searcher (Song et al., 2025). We additionally report LLM-as-Judge accuracy (ACCL) using Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026) to account for semantically correct answers that differ lexically from the reference. Appendix G.5 reports EM and SubEM. We also measure model-generated tokens and format validity where relevant.

Training and inference.

Qwen3.6-27B generates teacher trajectories used for joint Action/Edit SFT of LLaDA2.0-mini. MDSAS starts from the epoch-one SFT checkpoint, which also provides the frozen anchor. RL checkpoints are selected on a disjoint 256-question HotpotQA–2Wiki validation set. At inference, DiffuPlan uses greedy decoding with at most five top-3 retrievals. Additional hyperparameters and data construction details are in Appendices E and F.

4.2 End-to-End Search Performance

Table 1 evaluates overall answer quality. Under the semantic judge, DiffuPlan reaches 55.30 average ACCL, exceeding R1-Searcher by 2.70 points. Token F1 gives the same ranking: DiffuPlan obtains the highest average F1, 50.24, exceeding R1-Searcher by 1.53 points. It achieves the best score on all four datasets under both metrics. Gains on MuSiQue and Bamboogle show that the learned behavior transfers beyond the HotpotQA and 2Wiki domains used to construct teacher trajectories.

DLLM-Searcher produces substantially more verbose answer strings, which makes token F1 unusually harsh for that system. Under SubEM, the containment-style metric used in its evaluation setting, DiffuPlan still leads, 48.45 versus 36.25 (Appendix G.5). These results establish that editable-state diffusion search is competitive end-to-end; the following analyses test why.

5 Testing the Editable-State Hypothesis

5.1 Does Editable State Specifically Benefit Diffusion?

Our central hypothesis predicts an interaction effect: keeping one current plan should reduce redundant generation for either backbone, but direct reconstruction of earlier state should provide a larger accuracy benefit to the dLLM than to the AR model. Table 2 supports this prediction. On LLaDA2.0-mini, editable state improves average F1 from 47.80 to 50.24 (+2.44) and reduces model-generated tokens from 411 to 338 (18%). On Ling-mini-2.0, the same state protocol changes F1 from 49.54 to 50.01 (+0.47), despite a comparable token reduction from 425 to 357 (16%). The corresponding ACCL gains are +3.00 for the diffusion model and +1.10 for the AR model.

This comparison is important because both editable agents ultimately maintain the same current plan. The AR agent generates replacement text left-to-right and the controller writes it into the plan; the diffusion agent reconstructs the selected earlier span directly under full-canvas conditioning. Thus the much larger dLLM gain cannot be explained by retaining a single plan or by token savings alone. It is consistent with the hypothesis that bidirectional reconstruction supplies a better inductive bias for revising previously committed state from later observations. Although Ling-mini-2.0 scores slightly higher than LLaDA2.0-mini on general benchmarks (Bie et al., 2025), DiffuPlan is the most accurate and least costly of the four agents. Per-dataset results are reported in Appendix F.3.

5.2 Does the Gain Track the Need for Revision?

A second prediction is that editable state should matter little when no state revision is needed and matter increasingly as revision becomes more substantial. Figure 3 groups all 1,625 test questions by the append agent’s own edit requests, so the grouping is independent of DiffuPlan. The pattern is monotonic: editable state changes F1 by only +0.20 on questions with no edit request, by +2.79 when at least one edit is requested, by +4.63 when at least two updates are requested, and by +7.12 when replanning is requested. The editable agent also generates 5–30% fewer tokens in every group. Overall, DiffuPlan edits its state on 83% of test questions (Appendix F.4).

The accuracy trend is more informative than the efficiency gain alone. If the improvement came mainly from shorter outputs or from maintaining an explicit plan, we would not expect it to increase so sharply with the amount of required revision. Instead, the gain is concentrated precisely where later evidence most strongly changes earlier planning state.

5.3 Are EPM and Expansion Necessary?

Marginalizing equivalent expansion paths.

Figure 4(a) compares EPM with single-path cross-entropy while keeping dynamic expansion fixed. EPM improves validation EM from 31.64 to 42.19, F1 from 43.46 to 53.12, and format validity from 73.83% to 93.75%. The large gap supports the motivation for EPM: supervision should identify the desired replacement, not an arbitrary latent allocation of that replacement to expandable masks.

Allocating edit capacity dynamically.

Figure 4(b) compares dynamic expansion with a fixed 96-token edit canvas. Dynamic expansion raises F1 from 49.08 to 53.12 while preserving comparable format validity. This is not a rare corner case: 90.7% of executed edits on the test set invoke expansion (Appendix F.4). Variable-length state revision is therefore central to the practical protocol rather than an occasional fallback.

5.4 Optimizing the Agent without Losing the Protocol

With its frozen SFT anchor, MDSAS improves the SFT initialization from 53.12 to 58.98 validation F1. The anchor is essential for stable optimization: without it, hard-invalid rollouts rise to 99.8% by step 50 and validation F1 collapses to 2.08; with it, the hard-invalid fraction stays below 10% over the same interval (Appendix F.2). The best unanchored checkpoint reaches 55.81 F1, so the anchor improves not only late-stage stability but also the selected policy.

These results clarify the roles of the training components. SFT learns the editable-state protocol and the reconstruction operation; EPM makes variable-length revision learnable; and MDSAS improves multi-turn action selection, while its frozen SFT anchor keeps RL from destroying the executable protocol.

6 Conclusion

Current dLLM agents largely inherit an append-only interaction paradigm from autoregressive models, even though dLLMs can reconstruct earlier text from later context. DiffuPlan turns this unused capability into an agent-state primitive by maintaining one editable planning state and revising selected earlier spans as new evidence arrives. A shared Action/Edit model realizes forward acting and cross-turn reconstruction, while EPM learns variable-length edits without committing supervision to an arbitrary expansion path. Controlled experiments show that editable state improves the diffusion agent far more than its AR counterpart and that the gain increases with the amount of revision required. Together with strong end-to-end QA performance, these results suggest a broader design principle: diffusion agents need not simply reproduce AR-style interaction; they can exploit reconstruction to maintain state that remains revisable throughout interaction.

Limitations

Our study uses one diffusion backbone, LLaDA2.0-mini, and its AR source model, Ling-mini-2.0. Multi-turn RL over denoising trajectories requires repeated rollouts with retrieval at every turn, which limited the scale of our experiments; whether the advantage of editable state holds for larger dLLMs or other diffusion families remains untested. We evaluate only multi-hop open-domain QA over a fixed Wikipedia corpus, where plans are short and structured as indexed subquestions. Longer-horizon agents, such as coding agents or research agents with live web search, hold less structured state, and our marker-based controller would need to generalize to it. MDSAS optimizes when to edit but not the reconstruction itself, which stays as learned in SFT. Finally, SFT relies on trajectories from a larger teacher, Qwen3.6-27B, on two training domains, so the protocol it learns depends on the teacher’s search and revision behavior.

Appendix A Detailed Runtime

Algorithm 1 gives the complete execution loop, including the edit handoff between two Action-Mode segments. Each interaction produces one Action-Mode segment under the following grammar:

The grammar places a plan only in the initial segment and one terminal action after a non-empty think. Terminal answers must be concise. The runtime executes the first complete terminal action and requests a direct answer if none is available or an interaction budget is exhausted.

Appendix B Controller Implementation

B.1 Localize

The policy selects edit targets through markers; the controller localizes them without inferring which steps are solved. An update selects the first occurrence of each requested #A_i present in the plan. A replan with one matching #Q_i selects the suffix starting at that step; with multiple matching markers, it selects only the listed step spans. Unselected text is preserved.

B.2 Commit and history semantics

For an update, each selected answer marker is replaced by one logical mask. For a replan, all tokens overlapping the selected step spans are masked. The editor reconstructs these positions from the full interaction canvas, including subsequent actions and retrieved evidence. Commit propagates each decoded update value to all identical unresolved references and writes the revised plan back at its original position in the history.

The shared denoiser 𝒟θ\mathcal{D}_{\theta} reconstructs the masked spans of canvas XtX_{t}. The complete transition formalizes span selection, reconstruction, and commit as

St\displaystyle S_{t} =Γ⁡(Pt,at,ut),\displaystyle=\Gamma(P_{t},a_{t},u_{t}), (7)
(P~t,νt,ξt)\displaystyle(\widetilde{P}_{t},\nu_{t},\xi_{t}) =𝒟θ​(Mask⁡(Xt,St),Medit),\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}_{\theta}(\operatorname{Mask}(X_{t},S_{t});M^{\mathrm{edit}}),
Kt\displaystyle K_{t} =Close⁡(Pt,St,νt,at),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Close}(P_{t},S_{t},\nu_{t},a_{t}),
Pt+1\displaystyle P_{t+1} =Commit⁡(Pt,P~t,Kt,νt).\displaystyle=\operatorname{Commit}(P_{t},\widetilde{P}_{t},K_{t},\nu_{t}).

Here P~t\widetilde{P}_{t} is the candidate plan before reference propagation. The map νt\nu_{t} contains each selected update marker’s decoded value and is empty for replan. The commit closure KtK_{t} collects the spans changed by direct editing or reference propagation. It equals the selected replan spans; for an update, it additionally includes every identical marker occurrence reached by propagation. Commit preserves all other plan content. The denoiser returns status ξt∈{complete,stalled,max_steps}\xi_{t}\in\{\texttt{complete},\texttt{stalled},\texttt{max\_steps}\}. Missing plans or requests with no matching spans leave the history unchanged.

Each editable mask carries an owner label ω\omega. Expansion replaces it with two masks bearing the same label, keeping new positions attached to the originating span. Commit preserves all unselected plan content in order, including when expansion shifts subsequent token positions.

During rollout, we record the commit-step index ζg,j\zeta_{g,j} for each Action-Mode token yg,jy_{g,j}. D.3 Expansion runtime

An <EXPAND> prediction replaces one controller-owned mask by two masks with the same owner, increasing the canvas by one token. Each edit invocation permits at most Nexpmax=32N_{\mathrm{exp}}^{\max}=32 expansion events. The operator supports length-preserving and length-growing replacements; deletion and contraction are outside its scope.

Denoising stops when all owned masks are filled or the step limit Tmax=max⁡{1,|P|+2​Nexpmax+32}T_{\max}=\max\{1,|P|+2N_{\mathrm{exp}}^{\max}+32\} is reached, where |P||P| is the pre-edit plan length in tokens. Expansion is confined to controller-owned Edit-Mode positions.

Appendix E Teacher Data Construction

E.1 Teacher and sampling setup

Qwen3.6-27B generates trajectories with an indexed plan, retrieval, answer bindings, and replanning. Each retrieval returns three passages truncated to 500 whitespace-delimited words. Collection allows at most six searches, one replan, and two format-repair attempts; a second pass resamples first-pass rejections. The teacher decodes with temperature 0.5, top-pp 0.8, top-kk 20, and at most 1,024 output tokens.

E.2 Rejection sampling and canonicalization

We retain trajectories with token-level answer F1 above 0.650.65, at least one retrieval, and a valid plan–action structure. The converter maps each teacher trajectory into the two student views. Teacher answer bindings and rewritten questions become update Action records plus full-canvas Edit targets; teacher replacement suffixes become marker-only replan actions plus their corresponding Edit targets. Retrieved information remains conditioning context. Retrieval-limit records teach the agent to answer rather than issue another search.

Table 6 counts the canonical trajectories and derived records. Each canonical environment-facing decision yields one Action record. Each update or replan handoff yields multiple deduplicated DreamOn-style full-canvas corruption states (up to 12 per update and 24 per replan), explaining why Edit records outnumber both actions and trajectories.

Appendix F Full Training Details

F.1 Optimization configuration

We run SFT for two epochs and use the epoch-one checkpoint as the reported SFT policy and RL initialization. The training multiset 𝒟mix=𝒟mixact⊎𝒟mixedit\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{mix}}=\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{mix}}^{\mathrm{act}}\uplus\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{mix}}^{\mathrm{edit}} assigns multiplicity 1 to search, answer, and edit records, multiplicity 1.5 to updates, and multiplicity 3 to replans and search-limit recovery records. The joint SFT objective is

ℒSFT=1|𝒟mix|​[∑r∈𝒟mixactℓact​(r)+∑e∈𝒟mixeditℓedit​(e)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{mix}}|}\Bigl[\sum_{r\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{mix}}^{\mathrm{act}}}\ell_{\mathrm{act}}(r)+\sum_{e\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{mix}}^{\mathrm{edit}}}\ell_{\mathrm{edit}}(e)\Bigr]. (17)

Table 7 summarizes optimization.

Maximum sequence length is 4,096 and diffusion block size is 32. For an Action-Mode target yy,

σ∼𝒰⁡(0.3,0.8),mi∼Bernoulli⁡(σ),\sigma\sim\mathcal{U}(0.3,0.8),\qquad m_{i}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\sigma), (18)

and only target-segment tokens are eligible for corruption. If none is selected, one target position is forced to mask. Edit records receive no additional random corruption: controller ownership defines their EPM support.

F.2 MDSAS schedule and sampling

Training runs for 80 on-policy outer steps, sampling eight trajectories per question. PPO uses a clip of 0.150.15 and an old-policy KL coefficient of 0.020.02. The fixed SFT anchor has coefficient λSFT=0.02\lambda_{\mathrm{SFT}}=0.02. Each step makes one pass over the newly sampled Action-Mode rows. MDSAS uses a 2​N2N representation with 32-token blocks and shrink factor 8, which combines every eight distinct commit steps within a block into one training state. Table 11 lists the Action-Mode sampling parameters.

The RL training set consists of 4,030 examples sampled from the same training dataset used by R1-Searcher.

F.3 Backbone and protocol comparison

Section 5.1 trains the editable and append protocols on LLaDA2.0-mini and on Ling-mini-2.0. All four agents use the same Qwen3.6-27B teacher trajectories and record multiplicities, two SFT epochs with the epoch-one checkpoint, and the MDSAS schedule above, with RL checkpoints selected on the same 256-question validation set. Under the append protocol, teacher update and replan actions are serialized with the complete revised plan, and at inference the controller adds the generated plan to the history after the request without modifying the earlier plan. Under the editable protocol on Ling-mini-2.0, these actions carry the replacement text for the affected steps, written left to right, and the controller commits it into the planning state as for DiffuPlan, so the training histories of the two editable agents match token for token. Ling-mini-2.0 agents are served with vLLM, and all agents share the retriever and retrieval budget of Section 4.1. Table 8 reports the four agents on each dataset.

F.4 Edit usage at inference

Table 9 reports how often DiffuPlan edits its plan on the 1,625 test questions and how often the executed edits invoke expansion. Edit requests whose markers match no plan span leave the history unchanged and are not counted as executed edits. Table 10 pairs DiffuPlan with the LLaDA2.0-mini append agent of Table 2 on the same multi-hop questions, grouped by the append agent’s own edit requests.

Appendix G Evaluation Details

G.1 Retriever and corpus

All retrieval-based methods use intfloat/e5-base-v2 (Wang et al., 2022) with mean pooling over the Wiki18 corpus and FAISS inner-product search. Queries are truncated to 256 encoder tokens.

G.2 Prompts, answer extraction, and scoring

Direct, CoT, and Standard RAG use concise answer-tag prompts; other systems use their released or paper-specified workflows and native answer markers. A method-specific parser extracts the terminal answer. The common scorer lowercases text, removes punctuation and English articles, collapses whitespace, and takes the maximum score over reference aliases. EM compares normalized strings, token F1 measures token overlap, and SubEM tests whether a normalized reference appears in the prediction.

G.3 LLM-as-Judge

Lexical metrics penalize correct answers phrased differently from the references and reward responses that contain a reference without committing to it. We therefore also score every extracted answer with LLM-as-Judge, using Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026) as the judge model with thinking disabled and greedy decoding. The judge model receives the question, the reference aliases, and the extracted answer, truncated to 300 words, and returns a binary verdict. Its instructions treat aliases, abbreviations, name order, formatting differences, and additional correct detail as equivalent, and mark as incorrect an answer that is vaguer than every reference, names a different entity, lists several candidates, declares the answer unknown, contradicts a reference, or is empty; yes/no questions are compared by polarity only. Pooled over the twelve systems and 1,625 questions, the verdicts agree with EM on 86.5% of answers, with SubEM on 92.7%, and with nonzero F1 on 88.1%. Table 1 reports LLM-as-Judge accuracy beside F1 for every dataset, and Table 8 for the backbone and protocol comparison.

G.4 Format validity and reward gating

Format validity measures the fraction of trajectories with correct output structure, independently of answer correctness. The checks require an initial plan, balanced control tags, well-formed closing tags, a non-empty terminal answer without control markup, and valid reasoning–search transitions. Empty searches, duplicate answer blocks, and model-generated information blocks are invalid. Both SFT diagnostics in Figure 4(a,b) use this same definition.

For the RL reward gate in Equation 12, malformed control structures and missing or malformed terminal answers are hard-invalid. Edit-marker payloads are also checked for valid target syntax. Recoverable deviations, including an empty search or a missing reasoning transition between searches, are soft-invalid. The hard-invalid rollout rate in Figure 5 uses these training-time checks.

G.5 Answer-output metrics

EM and SubEM complement token F1 by measuring exact answers and the presence of a reference answer within the response; LLM-as-Judge (Appendix G.3) scores semantic correctness (Table 12).

Appendix H Qualitative Examples

The following traces retain every model action. Each Controller commit block shows a snapshot of the same plan after it has been edited in place. Only the retrieved passages inside <information> are abridged.

H.1 Successful update

For the question “Who wrote the 1897 novel about a vampire which was later turned into a 1931 film featuring Béla Ferenc Dezső Blaskó?”, the agent performs two successive updates:

⬇
Question: Who wrote the 1897 novel about a vampire which was later turned into a 1931 film featuring Bela Ferenc Dezso Blasko?
Student:
<plan>
#Q_1: Who is Bela Ferenc Dezso Blasko?
#Q_2: What 1931 film featuring #A_1 was based on an 1897 vampire novel?
#Q_3: Who wrote the 1897 novel #A_2?
</plan>
<think>I need to identify the actor Bela Ferenc Dezso Blasko to find the 1931 film he was in.</think>
<search>Bela Ferenc Dezso Blasko actor</search>
Environment (abridged):
<information>Bela Ferenc Dezso Blasko is better known as Bela Lugosi, the actor famous for portraying Count Dracula in the 1931 film.</information>
Student:
<think>The retrieved evidence states that Bela Ferenc Dezso Blasko is better known as Bela Lugosi.</think>
<update>#A_1</update>
Controller commit:
<plan>
#Q_1: Who is Bela Ferenc Dezso Blasko?
#Q_2: What 1931 film featuring Bela Lugosi was based on an 1897 vampire novel?
#Q_3: Who wrote the 1897 novel #A_2?
</plan>
Student:
<think>I need to identify the 1931 film featuring Bela Lugosi that was based on an 1897 vampire novel.</think>
<search>1931 film featuring Bela Lugosi based on 1897 vampire novel</search>
Environment (abridged):
<information>Dracula is a 1931 vampire film starring Bela Lugosi and based on the novel Dracula by Bram Stoker.</information>
Student:
<think>The retrieved information confirms that the 1931 film Dracula is based on the novel Dracula by Bram Stoker.</think>
<update>#A_2</update>
Controller commit:
<plan>
#Q_1: Who is Bela Ferenc Dezso Blasko?
#Q_2: What 1931 film featuring Bela Lugosi was based on an 1897 vampire novel?
#Q_3: Who wrote the 1897 novel Dracula?
</plan>
Student:
<think>I need to find the author of the 1897 novel Dracula.</think>
<search>author of 1897 novel Dracula</search>
Environment (abridged):
<information>Dracula is an 1897 Gothic horror novel by Irish author Bram Stoker.</information>
Student:
<think>The search results confirm that Bram Stoker is the author of the 1897 novel Dracula.</think>
<answer>Bram Stoker</answer>

The first commit binds the actor’s stage name into #Q_2; the second binds the film title into #Q_3. The final answer matches the reference, Bram Stoker.

H.2 Successful replan

For the question “Which 2009 film features an actor that also starred in Bad Samaritan?”, the agent first updates the cast binding and then replans after an incomplete retrieval:

⬇
Question: Which 2009 film features an actor that also starred in Bad Samaritan?
Student:
<plan>
#Q_1: Who are the main actors in Bad Samaritan?
#Q_2: Which 2009 film features #A_1?
</plan>
<think>I need to identify the cast of the film Bad Samaritan to find the actor in question.</think>
<search>Bad Samaritan film cast</search>
Environment (abridged):
<information>Bad Samaritan stars David Tennant and Robert Sheehan, with Carlito Olivero, Kerry Condon, and Jacqueline Byers.</information>
Student:
<think>The observation provides the evidence needed for the current step.</think>
<update>#A_1</update>
Controller commit:
<plan>
#Q_1: Who are the main actors in Bad Samaritan?
#Q_2: Which 2009 film features David Tennant or Robert Sheehan?
</plan>
Student:
<think>I will search for a 2009 film featuring either of these actors to find the answer.</think>
<search>2009 film starring David Tennant or Robert Sheehan</search>
Environment (abridged):
<information>Robert Sheehan appeared with Rupert Grint in an unnamed 2009 film set in Belfast; the retrieved text omits its title.</information>
Student:
<think>The observation provides the plot and co-star (Rupert Grint) for Robert Sheehan’s 2009 film but does not explicitly state the title. I will replan to search for the title using these constraints.</think>
<replan>#Q_2</replan>
Controller commit:
<plan>
#Q_1: Who are the main actors in Bad Samaritan?
#Q_2: What is the title of the 2009 film starring Robert Sheehan and Rupert Grint set in Belfast?
</plan>
Student:
<think>I will search for the title of the 2009 film starring Robert Sheehan and Rupert Grint.</think>
<search>2009 film starring Robert Sheehan and Rupert Grint set in Belfast</search>
Environment (abridged):
<information>Cherrybomb is a 2009 British drama starring Rupert Grint and Robert Sheehan and filmed in Belfast.</information>
Student:
<think>The observation provides the evidence needed for the current step.</think>
<answer>Cherrybomb</answer>

The replan preserves the resolved cast step and rewrites only #Q_2. The final answer matches the reference, Cherrybomb.
